Hope you are clear this time,

Thank you,

Best wishes,

Samundra

messages.body_plain:
Hi Samundra

John is right, and maybe that has answered your query (which should not have been posted in a 'stratified sampling' thread, but it's not easy to move now).

Also note -
1. It is wrong to refer to the habitat mask as ETA (effective trapping area). That concept (see Otis et al. 1978) is not relevant to spatially explicit capture-recapture.
2. The MCP of the cameras is also not relevant.
3. Although region.N may report a 'realised N' for a region smaller than the habitat mask, that number is almost meaningless as explained in Efford & Fewster: it is not reliable when some of the n detected animals may have been centred outside the region. 'expected N' is OK.
4. Whether region.N uses a derived density estimate (which, incidentally, uses g0 and sigma) or the parameter estimate D-hat from the fitted model, depends only on whether you fitted a model including D (i.e., CL = FALSE) or not (CL = TRUE).
5. In most cases the expected N is just the estimated density multiplied by the area of the region, so you can check the calculation by hand (the advantage of using region.N is that it gives a confidence interval).

I hope this helps.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
What we call 'realised N' is calculated by adding the number of actually detected animals n to a model-based estimate of the number of animals from the region of interest that were not detected.

Realised N is not defined and not computable if you cannot be sure that all the n animals belong in the region for which you wish to know N. If realised N is not defined then CL etc. for realised N are not defined. I cannot change that.

The solution is to use the 'expected N'. The wider CL honestly reflects the fact that you do not really know e.g., whether each tiger you are observe is Nepalese or Indian.

Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I have capture-recapture data for spotted hyaenas and leopards from camera trap surveys which took place over four sampling sessions (two wet and two dry seasons). Each session ran for 60 consecutive nights, however effort/usage for each session differs due to camera trap malfunctions. I have no problem creating the capthist file with different trap detector usages as seen below:

mydetectors <- c("S1_trapfile.csv", "S2_trapfile.csv", "S3_trapfile.csv", "S4_trapfile.csv")

SP_Left <- read.capthist("hyaenaleftcapturehist2.csv", mydetectors, detector = "proximity", fmt = "trapID",
trapcovnames =c( 'vegetation', 'elevation', 'slope', 'road', 'distancetowater'))

However, I am struggling to determine how to create the mask component of the secr.fit models. Using the game reserve boundary as a mask is not valid as we suspect that both leopards
and hyaenas could be moving in and out of the reserve (despite the reserve being fenced).

I used a constant mask (SPmask <- make.mask(traps(SP_Left), buffer = 3200, spacing = 1975, type = 'trapbuffer')) across all sessions for spotted hyaena by using MaxDM calculated from three
collared hyaenas and using the average space between camera traps. The population size estimates for the best fit model according to AIC is as seen below, which is was we expect
however, R.N gives NA values (which from a previous post I see isn't all bad):

> region.N(secrroad, region=SPmask, se.N=TRUE, aSPha=0.05)
[[1]]
    estimate SE.estimate      lcl      ucl  n

If I want to use MMDM per session as the buffer for spotted hyaenas or the RPSV values, firstly would this be correct and secondly how do I go about writing the code to incorporate a list
of values per session in making a mask?

Hope this all makes sense.

Kind regards,
Jess

Hi Jess

I'm not sure I quite get which N you want: is it the number of hyaenas/leopards centred within the reserve boundary? If that is the case then specify that a SpatialPolygonsDataFrame for the boundary as the region argument of region.N() (see ?region.N). messages.subject: Re: Extracting density variance
messages.body_plain:
The secr object returned by secr.fit() includes the variance-covariance matrix of the coefficients (beta parameters). This is displayed when you print an object of class 'secr'. You can extract it with the vcov method. For a simple model (no covariate or other effects on density) that is fitted by maximising the full likelihood (i.e. CL = FALSE) you can extract the variance of the density beta parameter with, for example,
vcov(secrdemo.0)[1,1]
With the default link (log), this is what you asked for (beta parameters always relate to the link scale). Life is more complex for more complex density models, and might involve some hacking of the predict.secr method to get at the variance of the linear predictor on the link scale. Best make sure you really want to do this before attempting...
Murray

messages.body_plain:
> Update:

The first error was due to my instinct to synchronize the dates of the telemetry and the trapping occasion - if a bird was tracked on October 10th, that was the 4th occasion during the trapping regimen, so I called it occasion 4 for the telemetry capture history. This left a whole bunch of zeroes for the telemetry capture history, which should not occur. I am not sure why I did this as it doesn't say to do so in any vignette. That said, it is fixed now.

The second error with "addTelemetry" is still an issue that I have not resolved. The only workaround that I have been able to try is "MS.capthist" which allows me to bind the two capture histories. I may be using it in the wrong context, as the telemetry data that I have is not from multiple sessions, but I am running some basic models with the combined capture history to give it a whirl.

Hope somebody in the future might find this useful!

Nathan W.

> The secr object returned by secr.fit() includes the variance-covariance matrix of the coefficients (beta parameters). This is displayed when you print an object of class 'secr'. You can extract it with the vcov method. For a simple model (no covariate or other effects on density) that is fitted by maximising the full likelihood (i.e. CL = FALSE) you can extract the variance of the density beta parameter with, for example,
> vcov(secrdemo.0)[1,1]
> With the default link (log), this is what you asked for (beta parameters always relate to the link scale). Life is more complex for more complex density models, and might involve some hacking of the predict.secr method to get at the variance of the linear predictor on the link scale. Best make sure you really want to do this before attempting...
